title: How the Senses Are Set as Rooms in the Body, and How the Lord Enters and Takes the Keys
reading:
When the natural mind was first being formed, it was the proprium that shaped it — organizing the body of Adam and Eve out of what it had claimed, working from the failed productions of self-love and yet imprinting upon them the likeness of the Lord's own call, because nothing can be made except after the divine pattern. The proprium saw the icon of the Lord summoning the rational, took its imprint, and pressed that imprint upon its molding. So the body itself, as the soul first finds it, is a vessel formed by self-claiming yet bearing in its very shape the trace of the One it claims to be from itself. It says, looking up at heaven: "Let us fashion an image after the likeness of the Exalted One" — and this is what self-love has always said, claiming as its own the form it could only receive.

Now within this molded body the proprium has set up faculties, one for each sense, and each faculty has its own house, with storehouses and granaries and inner chambers. Whatever the eye sees, whether beautiful or bitter, whether of love or of hate or of desire, is carried inward and laid up in those storehouses. The faculty watches over what it has gathered, and when something draws the heart to look again at what was seen, the faculty goes inward, retrieves the image from where it was kept, and produces it for whoever asks. So with hearing: every sound the ear takes in is carried inward, deposited, and watched over for many days, so that when one comes asking after that word, the faculty goes into its treasury and finds it and brings it out. So with smell, with taste, with the touch of the hands. Each of the five has its inner reservoir, each its watching, each its bringing forth on demand.

Above all five sits the heart, ruling them as a king rules. Whatever the five gather, they hand over to the heart as a deposit; and the heart watches over them, and when called for, sends them out and gives them. The heart's deliberation is like a king before whom the senators of his city stand, all matters laid before him; whatever his officers ask with strength, he grants out of those stores and the judgment by which they walk. He is also like a steward, who takes everything sent in and arranges it, vessel by vessel, place by place, so it can be found in the place where he has set it.

The body, then, is an encampment with gates, and the gates are the senses — the openings of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, speaking. At each gate stand watchmen and nets and guards. When something familiar comes, something that already belongs to the city of self-love, the watchmen open and bring it within according to the heart's purpose. But what is foreign to them they hinder; they do not let it cross the threshold. Or, if they do let it through, it is brought in only with great toil, through many cells where it is kept under their eye. The whole gating is in their hand, and what enters or does not enter depends on whether the watchmen recognize it as a fellow-citizen of the proprium or as a stranger.

This is the natural state. The faculty within — the teaching by which the body lives — is queen of the encampment under the heart's rule, and the gates open and shut at her pleasure. They open at the time of self-love's wishing, to take in the visions of pleasure and the chatter of cares and the tastes of defiled foods, drawing all of this inward toward the Sin within, which pulls the whole heart after itself.

But when the Lord comes ordering the rational — entering as truth that illumines the inner mind — and approaches the gates of the body, the proprium that holds those gates does not at first receive him. The watchmen call him a stranger and try to keep him out; they want only what is theirs. Yet he, in his wisdom and in his weight and in the multitude of his coming, humbles those guards. He brings them low. And when he has finished humbling them, he takes the keys out of their hands. The gates that until then opened only to fantasy and desire and the meditation of self-love's cares — those same gates now open and shut at his command. The body that was an encampment of the proprium becomes a dwelling under the Lord's ordering, and the senses that gathered for self-love now gather for the recognition of what flows through them as his.
